claim: Type 1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1Rs) are widely expressed in the vertebrate retina.
source: Type 1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1Rs) are widely expressed in the vertebrate retina, but the role of endocannabinoids in vision is not fully understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established context for the study.

claim: CB1R activation reduces intracellular Cl− levels in RGCs through AMPK-dependent inhibition of NKCC1 activity.
source: Clomeleon imaging and patch clamp recordings revealed that inhibition of NKCC1 downstream of CB1R activation reduces intracellular Cl− levels in RGCs, hyperpolarizing the resting membrane potential.
evidence: The abstract describes experimental findings from Clomeleon imaging and patch clamp recordings.

claim: Hyperpolarization of RGCs enhances action potential firing in response to subsequent depolarization.
source: We confirmed that such hyperpolarization enhances RGC action potential firing in response to subsequent depolarization, consistent with the increased intrinsic excitability of RGCs observed with CB1R activation.
evidence: The abstract states this was confirmed experimentally.

claim: CB1R activation markedly improves visual contrast sensitivity under low-light conditions in freely swimming Xenopus tadpoles.
source: Using a dot avoidance assay in freely swimming Xenopus tadpoles, we demonstrate that CB1R activation markedly improves visual contrast sensitivity under low-light conditions.
evidence: The abstract describes behavioral assay results demonstrating improved visual contrast sensitivity.

claim: Endocannabinoids are lipid-derived regulators of synaptic transmission that serve as important mediators of functional plasticity.
source: Endocannabinoids (eCBs) are lipid-derived regulators of synaptic transmission that serve as important mediators of functional plasticity (Bellocchio et al., 2013; Bender et al., 2006; Clapper et al., 2010; El Manira and Kyriakatos, 2010; Han et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2012; Sjöström et al., 2003) and nervous system development (Argaw et al., 2011; Berghuis et al., 2007; Harkany et al., 2008; Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: High levels of CB1Rs and eCB production and degradation machinery have been found in all vertebrate retinal models tested.
source: In the retina, high levels of type 1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1R), as well as the eCB production and degradation machinery, have been found in all vertebrate models tested, and within nearly all retinal cell types throughout development and adulthood (Straiker et al., 1999; Yazulla, 2008; Zabouri et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: eCB modulation of voltage-dependent Ca2+ and K+ conductances typically results in downregulation of neurotransmitter release.
source: Although eCB modulation of voltage-dependent Ca2+ and K+ conductances, typically resulting in the downregulation of neurotransmitter release, has been demonstrated at multiple stages of retinal processing from photoreceptors to retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) (Fan and Yazulla, 2003; Lalonde et al., 2006; Middleton and Protti, 2011; Yazulla et al., 2000), these observations have not been directly linked to specific perceptual outcomes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Cannabis consumption in humans has been reported to positively modulate contrast discrimination.
source: On the other hand, cannabis consumption in humans has been reported to positively modulate contrast discrimination (Russo et al., 2004; West, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CB1R is present in the brain of adult Xenopus laevis frogs.
source: The presence of CB1Rs has been reported in the brain of the adult Xenopus laevis frog (Cesa et al., 2001; Cottone et al., 2003) and in the tadpole olfactory bulb (Breunig et al., 2010; Czesnik et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CB1R immunoreactivity is present in the outer and inner plexiform layers of Xenopus tadpole retinae.
source: We examined the retinae of Xenopus tadpoles, and found intense CB1R immunoreactivity (CB1R-IR) in the outer and inner plexiform layers (Figure 1a,b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with reports in other species (Middleton and Protti, 2011; Yazulla et al., 2000; Zabouri et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1 and citations to prior studies.

claim: Somatic CB1R immunoreactivity has been described in RGCs of salamander and chick but not in rat.
source: Somatic CB1R-IR has been described in the RGCs of salamander and chick (Straiker et al., 1999), but not in rat (Yazulla et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CB1R immunoreactivity is associated with GFP-positive RGCs in Isl2b:GFP transgenic frogs.
source: Using Isl2b:GFP transgenic frogs, in which expression of green fluorescent protein (GFP) in the retina is restricted to RGCs, we found CB1R-IR associated with GFP-positive RGCs in histological sections (Figure 1c) and in overnight dissociated retinal cultures (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1c and 1d.

claim: WIN 55,212-2 application increased RGC spiking rates in response to full field light-ON stimuli.
source: Extracellular multi-unit recordings in isolated eye preparations (Figure 2a) revealed that application of the CB1R agonist WIN 55,212-2 (1 µM) increased spiking rates of RGCs in response to both full field light-ON (before: 34.2 ± 3.1 Hz, after: 43.3 ± 4.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.010, two-way RM ANOVA) and light-OFF (before: 37.2 ± 3.1 Hz, after: 45.2 ± 4.2 Hz, n = 10, p=0.011) stimuli (Figure 2b,c; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,d).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 2.

claim: WIN 55,212-2 application increased RGC spiking rates in response to full field light-OFF stimuli.
source: Extracellular multi-unit recordings in isolated eye preparations (Figure 2a) revealed that application of the CB1R agonist WIN 55,212-2 (1 µM) increased spiking rates of RGCs in response to both full field light-ON (before: 34.2 ± 3.1 Hz, after: 43.3 ± 4.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.010, two-way RM ANOVA) and light-OFF (before: 37.2 ± 3.1 Hz, after: 45.2 ± 4.2 Hz, n = 10, p=0.011) stimuli (Figure 2b,c; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,d).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 2.

claim: ACEA enhanced RGC spiking to light-OFF stimuli.
source: This cannabinoid-mediated enhancement of evoked RGC responses was confirmed using a different CB1R agonist arachidonyl-2'-chloroethylamide (ACEA, 1 µM) which gave a similar enhancement of spiking to light-OFF stimuli (Figure 2d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,e; before: 30.5 ± 4.1 Hz, after: 40.0 ± 6.0 Hz, n = 10, p=0.033).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: URB597 treatment caused elevated spiking rates in response to light-ON stimulation.
source: URB597 treatment caused elevated spiking rates in response to light-ON (before: 22.8 ± 5.3 Hz, after: 31.3 ± 6.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.049) and light-OFF stimulation (Figure 2e; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,f; before: 51.0 ± 7.0 Hz; after: 61.7 ± 10.3 Hz, n = 10, p=0.031), suggesting that AEA synthesized in the retina is able to modulate visual responses.
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: URB597 treatment caused elevated spiking rates in response to light-OFF stimulation.
source: URB597 treatment caused elevated spiking rates in response to light-ON (before: 22.8 ± 5.3 Hz, after: 31.3 ± 6.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.049) and light-OFF stimulation (Figure 2e; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,f; before: 51.0 ± 7.0 Hz; after: 61.7 ± 10.3 Hz, n = 10, p=0.031), suggesting that AEA synthesized in the retina is able to modulate visual responses.
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: AEA synthesized in the retina is able to modulate visual responses.
source: URB597 treatment caused elevated spiking rates in response to light-ON (before: 22.8 ± 5.3 Hz, after: 31.3 ± 6.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.049) and light-OFF stimulation (Figure 2e; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,f; before: 51.0 ± 7.0 Hz; after: 61.7 ± 10.3 Hz, n = 10, p=0.031), suggesting that AEA synthesized in the retina is able to modulate visual responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the URB597 experimental results.

claim: WIN 55,212-2 perfusion did not produce significant changes in the amplitudes of the a-, b- or d-waves in ERG recordings.
source: However, perfusion of WIN 55,212-2 did not produce any significant changes in the amplitudes of the a-, b- or d-waves in response to step increments or decrements of light (Figure 2g, n = 6, 6, 6, 6; p=0.78, 0.79, 0.89, 0.68, two-way RM ANOVA), suggesting that CB1R activation does not impact light-evoked activity in the outer part of the retina, consistent with a recent report in the mouse (Cécyre et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by ERG recording data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: CB1R activation does not impact light-evoked activity in the outer part of the retina.
source: However, perfusion of WIN 55,212-2 did not produce any significant changes in the amplitudes of the a-, b- or d-waves in response to step increments or decrements of light (Figure 2g, n = 6, 6, 6, 6; p=0.78, 0.79, 0.89, 0.68, two-way RM ANOVA), suggesting that CB1R activation does not impact light-evoked activity in the outer part of the retina, consistent with a recent report in the mouse (Cécyre et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the ERG data and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: CB1R activation did not increase bipolar axon Ca2+ transient amplitude in response to light-ON stimulation.
source: Comparing average peak Ca2+ transients evoked by full-field light-ON and light-OFF stimulation before and after WIN 55,212-2 perfusion (Figure 3c), we found that CB1R activation did not increase bipolar axon Ca2+ transient amplitude in response to visual stimulation, but instead decreased it in the case of light-OFF stimulation (Figure 3d,e, ON: n = 10, p=0.17, OFF: n = 10, p=0.002), consistent with reports from salamander of a CB1R-mediated reduction of the L-type Ca2+ current12.
evidence: This is supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CB1R activation decreased bipolar axon Ca2+ transient amplitude in response to light-OFF stimulation.
source: Comparing average peak Ca2+ transients evoked by full-field light-ON and light-OFF stimulation before and after WIN 55,212-2 perfusion (Figure 3c), we found that CB1R activation did not increase bipolar axon Ca2+ transient amplitude in response to visual stimulation, but instead decreased it in the case of light-OFF stimulation (Figure 3d,e, ON: n = 10, p=0.17, OFF: n = 10, p=0.002), consistent with reports from salamander of a CB1R-mediated reduction of the L-type Ca2+ current12.
evidence: This is supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Peak Ca2+ transients in amacrine cell terminals evoked by light-ON and light-OFF stimulation were not significantly different before and after WIN 55,212-2 perfusion.
source: Peak Ca2+ transients in amacrine cell terminals evoked by light-ON and light-OFF stimulation were not significantly different before and after WIN 55,212-2 perfusion (Figure 3f–i, ON: n = 10, p=0.36; OFF: n = 10, p=0.48).
evidence: This is supported by GCaMP6s imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Application of WIN 55,212-2 resulted in a significant decrease in the total integrated EPSC in RGCs.
source: Application of WIN 55,212-2 resulted in a significant decrease in the total integrated EPSC, measured over 1 s following stimulus onset (Figure 3m,n, n = 7, p=0.025, two-way RM ANOVA, before vs. +WIN simple effect).
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Inhibitory synaptic input in response to light-ON stimuli was unchanged by WIN 55,212-2.
source: Inhibitory synaptic input in response to light-ON stimuli was unchanged by WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 3o, n = 5, p=0.199, two-way RM ANOVA with Holm-Sidak posthoc test) but a decrease in the total integrated IPSC in response to light-OFF stimulation was observed (Figure 3p, n = 5, p=0.029).
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A decrease in the total integrated IPSC in response to light-OFF stimulation was observed with WIN 55,212-2.
source: Inhibitory synaptic input in response to light-ON stimuli was unchanged by WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 3o, n = 5, p=0.199, two-way RM ANOVA with Holm-Sidak posthoc test) but a decrease in the total integrated IPSC in response to light-OFF stimulation was observed (Figure 3p, n = 5, p=0.029).
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 3.

claim: AM-251 pretreatment completely prevented the potentiating effects of WIN 55,212-2 on RGC firing.
source: Pretreatment with the CB1R blocker AM-251 (5 µM) completely prevented the potentiating effects of WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 4a, n = 10, p=0.487, one-tailed one-way RM ANOVA) or ACEA (Figure 4b, n = 10, p=0.360) on RGC firing, further underscoring the requirement for CB1R activation.
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: AM-251 pretreatment prevented the potentiating effects of ACEA on RGC firing.
source: Pretreatment with the CB1R blocker AM-251 (5 µM) completely prevented the potentiating effects of WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 4a, n = 10, p=0.487, one-tailed one-way RM ANOVA) or ACEA (Figure 4b, n = 10, p=0.360) on RGC firing, further underscoring the requirement for CB1R activation.
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: AM-251 prevented the enhancement caused by elevating endogenous AEA using URB597.
source: The enhancement produced by elevating endogenous AEA using URB597 (Figure 2e) was also prevented by AM-251 (Figure 4c, n = 10, p=0.500).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Gabazine did not prevent the WIN 55,212-2-induced increase in RGC firing in response to light.
source: The selective GABA-A receptor blocker gabazine (6 µM) had no specific effect on visually-evoked spike rates and did not prevent the WIN 55,212-2-induced increase in RGC firing in response to light (Figure 4d, n = 10, p=0.012).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Strychnine prevented the enhancement caused by WIN 55,212-2 application.
source: However, strychnine (60 µM), a potent and selective antagonist of glycine receptors (GlyRs) prevented (Figure 4e, n = 10, p=0.423) and reversed (Figure 4f, n = 10, p=0.044) the enhancement caused by WIN 55,212-2 application.
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4e and 4f.

claim: Strychnine reversed the enhancement caused by WIN 55,212-2 application.
source: However, strychnine (60 µM), a potent and selective antagonist of glycine receptors (GlyRs) prevented (Figure 4e, n = 10, p=0.423) and reversed (Figure 4f, n = 10, p=0.044) the enhancement caused by WIN 55,212-2 application.
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Both CB1Rs and GlyRs are required for the cannabinoid-mediated increase in RGC response to visual stimulation.
source: These results show that both CB1Rs and GlyRs are required for the cannabinoid-mediated increase in RGC response to visual stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological experiments with AM-251 and strychnine.

claim: NKCC1 and KCC2 mRNAs are expressed in stage 45 Xenopus retina.
source: NKCC1 and KCC2 are co-expressed in RGCs in fish retina (Dmitriev et al., 2007), and we were able to detect both mRNAs in stage 45 Xenopus retina (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Perfusion of bumetanide alone was sufficient to increase the firing rates of RGCs in response to light.
source: Perfusion of the selective NKCC1 inhibitor bumetanide (10 µM) alone was sufficient to increase the firing rates of RGCs in response to light, mimicking the effect of CB1R activation (Figure 4g, n = 10, p=0.025).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Subsequent addition of WIN 55,212-2 in the presence of bumetanide produced no additional increase in RGC firing rate.
source: Subsequent addition of WIN 55,212-2 in the presence of bumetanide produced no additional increase in RGC firing rate (n = 10, p=0.224).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data.

claim: WIN 55,212-2 application occluded the increase in RGC firing rate produced by adding bumetanide.
source: Furthermore, WIN 55,212-2 application (Figure 4h, n = 9, p=0.012) occluded the increase in RGC firing rate produced by adding bumetanide (Figure 4h, n = 9, p=0.224 vs. WIN alone).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: CB1R activation may work by regulating NKCC1 function to modulate the driving force of chloride currents in RGCs.
source: These results argue that CB1R activation may work by regulating NKCC1 function to modulate the driving force of chloride currents in RGCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the bumetanide occlusion experiments.

claim: WIN 55,212-2 application produced a striking increase in the levels of phosphorylated SPAK/OSR1.
source: We examined the involvement of these regulatory molecules by performing western blotting on retina homogenates from animals treated with WIN 55,212-2. WIN 55,212-2 application produced a striking increase in the levels of phosphorylated SPAK/OSR1, indicating its activation downstream of the CB1R (Figure 4j,k); however, this was not accompanied by an increase in phospho-NKCC1T212/T217 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4j and 4k.

claim: WIN 55,212-2 application was not accompanied by an increase in phospho-NKCC1T212/T217.
source: We examined the involvement of these regulatory molecules by performing western blotting on retina homogenates from animals treated with WIN 55,212-2. WIN 55,212-2 application produced a striking increase in the levels of phosphorylated SPAK/OSR1, indicating its activation downstream of the CB1R (Figure 4j,k); however, this was not accompanied by an increase in phospho-NKCC1T212/T217 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Dorsomorphin reversed the effects of WIN 55,212-2, reducing RGC spiking rate in response to light-OFF flashes.
source: We found that dorsomorphin (10 µM) reversed the effects of WIN 55,212-2, reducing RGCs spiking rate in response to light-OFF flashes (before: 37.5 ± 6.3 Hz, after: 22.9 ± 2.6 Hz, Figure 4l, n = 10, p=0.0095, paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 4l.

claim: CB1R signaling inhibits NKCC1 through the activation of AMPK.
source: These results indicate that CB1R signaling inhibits NKCC1 through the activation of AMPK.
evidence: This is inferred from the dorsomorphin experiment.

claim: CB1R activation consistently caused a rapid decrease in the cyan:yellow emission ratio in RGCs indicating a reduction in [Cl−]i.
source: In all experiments, CB1R activation consistently caused a rapid decrease in the cyan:yellow emission ratio in RGCs (Figure 5d,e, n = 15 cells, p=0.001, two-way RM ANOVA with Holm-Sidak post-test) indicating a reduction in [Cl−]i.
evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: No FRET changes in amacrine, bipolar or Müller glia cell types were detected with CB1R activation.
source: No FRET changes in amacrine (n = 16, p=0.649), bipolar (n = 12, p=0.972) or Müller glia (n = 8, p=0.997) cell types were detected (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The decrease in the cyan:yellow emission ratio in RGCs was not observed when expressing a control Cl−-insensitive Clomeleon-M69Q construct.
source: The decrease in the cyan:yellow emission ratio in RGCs was not observed when expressing a control Cl−-insensitive Clomeleon-M69Q construct (Figure 5f, n = 5, p=0.996).
evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Pretreatment with AM-251 prevented changes in [Cl−]i upon addition of WIN 55,212-2.
source: Pretreatment with AM-251 (n = 8) or bumetanide (n = 9) prevented any changes in [Cl−]i upon addition of WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 5f, p=0.996 for both).
evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Pretreatment with bumetanide prevented changes in [Cl−]i upon addition of WIN 55,212-2.
source: Pretreatment with AM-251 (n = 8) or bumetanide (n = 9) prevented any changes in [Cl−]i upon addition of WIN 55,212-2 (Figure 5f, p=0.996 for both).
evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: CB1R activation induces a RGC-specific decrease in [Cl−]i by regulating NKCC1 activity.
source: These data suggest that CB1R activation induces a RGC-specific decrease in [Cl−]i by regulating NKCC1 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the Clomeleon imaging experiments.

claim: With synaptic block, WIN 55,212-2 application still significantly decreased the cyan:yellow ratio in RGCs.
source: To determine if synaptic activity might contribute to the changes in [Cl−]i, we blocked synaptic transmission with a cocktail of DNQX (20 µM), AP4 (50 µM), picrotoxin (100 µM), strychnine (60 µM) and TTX (1 µM). With synaptic block, WIN 55,212-2 application still significantly decreased the cyan:yellow ratio in RGCs (Figure 5g, n = 14, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Retinal CB1R activation rapidly decreases [Cl−]i specifically in RGCs through a NKCC1-dependent and neurotransmission-independent mechanism.
source: These data indicate that retinal CB1R activation rapidly decreases [Cl−]i specifically in RGCs through a NKCC1-dependent and neurotransmission-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the synaptic block experiments.

claim: A small but significant leftward shift for EGly could be seen following wash-on of WIN 55,212-2.
source: We measured EGly by generating current-voltage (I-V) plots of peak current evoked by a brief application of glycine (500 µM for 20 ms) over a range of holding potentials (Figure 6e). A small but significant leftward shift for EGly could be seen following wash-on of WIN 55,212-2 in the bath (∆V = −3.2 ± 0.8 mV, n = 7, p=0.008).
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Inhibition of NKCC1 with bath application of bumetanide produced a similar shift in EGly.
source: Inhibition of NKCC1 with bath application of bumetanide produced a similar shift in EGly (Figure 6f, ∆V = −1.6 ± 0.5 mV, n = 5, p=0.026).
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp recording data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Application of WIN 55,212-2 significantly hyperpolarized RGCs in dissociated cultures.
source: Application of WIN 55,212-2 significantly hyperpolarized RGCs (Figure 6h, uncorrected for liquid junction potential; n = 6, p=0.004, paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by gramicidin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 6h.

claim: The WIN 55,212-2-induced hyperpolarization was prevented in the presence of AM-251.
source: This shift was prevented in the presence of AM-251 (Figure 6i, n = 6, p=0.14, one-way RM ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by gramicidin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 6i.

claim: CB1R-mediated hyperpolarization does not depend on cannabinoid actions on other cells in the retina.
source: This experiment not only confirms that CB1R activation can hyperpolarize RGCs, but the fact that it does so in isolated cells, shows that this effect does not depend on cannabinoid actions on other cells in the retina.
evidence: This is inferred from the dissociated cell experiments.

claim: RGCs decrease their excitability following a period of depolarization and firing through the inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels.
source: RGCs are known to decrease their excitability following a period of depolarization and firing through the inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels as a way of extending their dynamic range (Kim and Rieke, 2001, 2003; Weick and Demb, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The number of spikes evoked by the test pulse was substantially elevated following hyperpolarizing pre-pulses.
source: The number of spikes evoked by the test pulse was substantially elevated following hyperpolarizing pre-pulses, whereas it decreased after depolarizing pre-pulses (Figure 6k).
evidence: This is supported by current clamp recording data shown in Figure 6k.

claim: The number of spikes evoked by the test pulse decreased after depolarizing pre-pulses.
source: The number of spikes evoked by the test pulse was substantially elevated following hyperpolarizing pre-pulses, whereas it decreased after depolarizing pre-pulses (Figure 6k).
evidence: This is supported by current clamp recording data shown in Figure 6k.

claim: eCBs can be released from neurons in response to stimulation driving a prolonged increase in intracellular Ca2+.
source: eCBs can be released from neurons in response to stimulation driving a prolonged increase in intracellular Ca2+ (Hashimotodani et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Sustained peripheral illumination elevated the RGC spike rate evoked by light-OFF test stimuli in the central subfield.
source: In a significant majority of cases, sustained peripheral illumination elevated the RGC spike rate evoked by light-OFF test stimuli in the central subfield (Figure 7e, before: 4.2 ± 1.6 Hz, after: 8.8 ± 2.4 Hz, n = 10, p=0.042, paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The effects of conditioning stimulation were prevented by bath application of AM-251.
source: Furthermore, the effects of conditioning stimulation were prevented by bath application of AM-251 (before: 6.9 ± 2.8 Hz, after: 4.7 ± 1.6 Hz, n = 10, p=0.244) (Figure 7b,d,f), consistent with a CB1R-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Conditioning with peripheral field stimulation induced a CB1R-dependent decrease of [Cl−]i in RGCs.
source: As predicted by our model, conditioning with peripheral field stimulation also induced a CB1R-dependent decrease of [Cl−]i in RGCs.
evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging experiments.

claim: A significant reduction in [Cl−]i compared with baseline was observed in RGCs in response to conditioning stimulation.
source: In response, we observed a significant reduction in [Cl−]i compared with baseline in RGCs (Figure 7i, n = 22, p=0.0004, two-way RM ANOVA), and this effect was blocked by pre-treatment with AM-251 (Figure 7j, n = 17, p=0.903).
evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 7i.

claim: The conditioning-induced reduction in [Cl−]i in RGCs was blocked by pre-treatment with AM-251.
source: In response, we observed a significant reduction in [Cl−]i compared with baseline in RGCs (Figure 7i, n = 22, p=0.0004, two-way RM ANOVA), and this effect was blocked by pre-treatment with AM-251 (Figure 7j, n = 17, p=0.903).
evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 7j.

claim: No significant reduction in [Cl−]i was found in amacrine or bipolar cells immediately following the conditioning stimulation.
source: In contrast, we did not find any significant reduction in [Cl−]i in amacrine (n = 19, p=0.903) or bipolar (n = 10, p=0.831) cells immediately following the conditioning stimulation (Figure 7k).
evidence: This is supported by Clomeleon imaging data shown in Figure 7k.

claim: CB1R activation can occur naturally in the retina in response to sustained illumination in peripheral visual fields.
source: Taken together, these data show that CB1R activation can occur naturally in the retina in response to sustained illumination in peripheral visual fields, and it appears to increase the number of RGCs responding to test stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the conditioning stimulation experiments.

claim: Following bath application of WIN 55,212-2, peak amplitudes of retinal evoked EPSCs were significantly increased.
source: Direct electrical stimulation of RGCs through a glass-stimulating electrode placed in the ganglion cell layer of the eye (Figure 8a) evoked α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptor-mediated retinotectal currents with latencies of about 5 ms in postsynaptic tectal neurons clamped at −60 mV. Following bath application (perfusion over the entire tadpole) of WIN 55,212-2 (1 µM), peak amplitudes of retinal evoked EPSCs were significantly increased (Figure 8b,c; 151.9 ± 17.5% baseline, n = 11, p=0.0004).
evidence: This is supported by amphotericin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The increase in EPSC amplitude was dependent on CB1R activation, as it was blocked by AM-251.
source: This increase in EPSC amplitude was dependent on CB1R activation, as it was blocked by the inverse agonist AM-251 (Figure 8c, n = 5, p=0.497).
evidence: This is supported by amphotericin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Increasing the endogenous AEA concentration with URB597 increased EPSC amplitude.
source: Increasing the endogenous AEA concentration with URB597 similarly increased EPSC amplitude (Figure 8c, n = 7, p=0.029).
evidence: This is supported by amphotericin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Treatments with NAM or JZL184 showed no enhancement of EPSC amplitude.
source: Treatments with either N-arachidonyl maleimide (NAM, 150 nM, n = 7, p=0.988) or JZL184 (100 nM, n = 7, p=0.999), two selective inhibitors of monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL), the 2-AG degrading enzyme, showed no enhancement (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a), providing further evidence that AEA is likely to be the endogenous cannabinoid that mediates the augmentation of the response to retinal stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by amphotericin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1a.

claim: AEA is likely to be the endogenous cannabinoid that mediates the augmentation of the response to retinal stimulation.
source: Treatments with either N-arachidonyl maleimide (NAM, 150 nM, n = 7, p=0.988) or JZL184 (100 nM, n = 7, p=0.999), two selective inhibitors of monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL), the 2-AG degrading enzyme, showed no enhancement (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a), providing further evidence that AEA is likely to be the endogenous cannabinoid that mediates the augmentation of the response to retinal stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of MAGL inhibitors.

claim: The WIN 55,212-2-induced enhancement of retinotectal EPSC amplitudes were blocked by strychnine and bumetanide.
source: The WIN 55,212-2-induced enhancement of retinotectal EPSC amplitudes were blocked by strychnine and bumetanide (Figure 8—figure supplement 1b), mirroring their effects on RGCs recorded in the isolated retinal eyecup (Figure 4e–h) and suggesting that the changes in RGC excitability probably underlie the enhanced retinotectal responses to stimulation in the eye.
evidence: This is supported by amphotericin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The changes in RGC excitability probably underlie the enhanced retinotectal responses to stimulation in the eye.
source: The WIN 55,212-2-induced enhancement of retinotectal EPSC amplitudes were blocked by strychnine and bumetanide (Figure 8—figure supplement 1b), mirroring their effects on RGCs recorded in the isolated retinal eyecup (Figure 4e–h) and suggesting that the changes in RGC excitability probably underlie the enhanced retinotectal responses to stimulation in the eye.
evidence: This is inferred from the parallel effects of strychnine and bumetanide on RGCs and retinotectal responses.

claim: The difference in peak amplitude before and after WIN 55,212-2 application could no longer be detected in isolated brain preparation.
source: To determine whether CB1R agonist perfusion was enhancing responses through action in the eye or in the tectum, we used an isolated brain preparation in which the eyes were no longer present and instead stimulated the severed RGC axons in the optic tract directly using a bipolar-stimulating electrode (Wu et al., 1996). The difference in the peak amplitude before and after WIN 55,212-2 application could no longer be detected (Figure 8d, 100 ± 11% baseline, n = 7, p=0.999).
evidence: This is supported by amphotericin-perforated patch recording data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: The cannabinoid-mediated enhancement of retinotectal EPSC amplitude is due to increased retinal excitability rather than to changes at the retinotectal synapses or in properties of the neurons within the optic tectum.
source: This indicates that the cannabinoid-mediated enhancement of retinotectal EPSC amplitude is due to increased retinal excitability and the resulting recruitment of more RGCs when stimulating in the eye, rather than to changes at the retinotectal synapses or in properties of the neurons within the optic tectum (Figure 8—figure supplement 1c–h).
evidence: This is inferred from the isolated brain preparation experiment.

claim: WIN 55,212-2 application produced a significant increase in tectal RF size.
source: WIN 55,212-2 application produced a significant increase in tectal RF size (127.6 ± 9.4% baseline, n = 5, p=0.042, one-sample t-test) and in the total charge evoked (140.3 ± 14.2% baseline, n = 5, p=0.047) across all responsive subfields (Figure 8f–h).
evidence: This is supported by receptive field mapping data shown in Figure 8.

claim: WIN 55,212-2 application produced a significant increase in the total charge evoked across all responsive subfields.
source: WIN 55,212-2 application produced a significant increase in tectal RF size (127.6 ± 9.4% baseline, n = 5, p=0.042, one-sample t-test) and in the total charge evoked (140.3 ± 14.2% baseline, n = 5, p=0.047) across all responsive subfields (Figure 8f–h).
evidence: This is supported by receptive field mapping data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Activation of retinal CB1Rs increases the size and strength of tectal RFs, most likely through the recruitment of responses from initially subthreshold RGC inputs.
source: These results show that activation of retinal CB1Rs increases the size and strength of tectal RFs, most likely through the recruitment of responses from initially subthreshold RGC inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the receptive field mapping experiments.

claim: WIN 55,212-2 treatment did not impair basic motor coordination.
source: Importantly, WIN 55,212-2 treatment did not impair basic motor coordination. The mean velocities of swimming tadpoles when not interacting with dots was indistinguishable between control and WIN 55,212-2-treated groups, indicating that the drug did not alter the rhythms or coordination underlying swimming behavior (Figure 8k, n = 24, p=0.491, two-way RM ANOVA with Holm-Sidak posttest).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 8k.

claim: WIN 55,212-2-treated tadpoles swam significantly faster when executing escape behaviors.
source: However, we did find that WIN 55,212-2-treated tadpoles swam significantly faster when executing escape behaviors (n = 24, p<0.001), highlighting the caveat that higher-order circuitry was likely also affected by the drug treatments.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 8k.

claim: Under photopic conditions, control tadpoles and WIN 55,212-2-treated tadpoles did not differ in their avoidance response rates to dots of various luminances.
source: When dark dots were presented under photopic conditions (overall luminance of the field = 190 cd m−2), control tadpoles and WIN 55,212-2-treated tadpoles did not differ in their avoidance response rates to dots having a luminance 190, 150 and 90 cd m−2 darker than background. All elicited significantly more escapes than the false-positive rate measured during the pre-test periods. The faintest dots, which differed from background by only 16 cd m−2, did not elicit a significant reaction (Figure 8l).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 8l.

claim: Under mesopic light conditions, control animals responded only at chance levels to all stimuli tested.
source: Under mesopic light conditions (overall luminance of the field = 0.65 cd m−2) control animals responded only at chance levels to all stimuli tested.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tracking data.

claim: WIN 55,212-2-treated tadpoles successfully avoided a significant fraction of dots with luminance differences to the background as small as 0.22 cd m−2 under mesopic conditions.
source: Remarkably, WIN 55,212-2-treated tadpoles successfully avoided a significant fraction of dots with luminance differences to the background as small as 0.22 cd m−2 (Figure 8m, n = 24, p=0.003, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 8m.

claim: Tadpoles treated with URB597 showed significantly enhanced dot avoidance compared to untreated controls.
source: Furthermore, tadpoles treated with URB597 to elevate endogenous cannabinoid levels also showed significantly enhanced dot avoidance compared to untreated controls (Figure 8n, n = 24, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 8n.

claim: The effects of URB597 were abolished by the CB1R inverse agonist AM-251.
source: The effects of URB597 were abolished by the CB1R inverse agonist AM-251 (5 µM), indicating that the drug was indeed acting by elevating endogenous cannabinoids (n = 24, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tracking data.

claim: Endogenous AEA acting on CB1Rs is able to enhance visual contrast sensitivity.
source: These results demonstrate that endogenous AEA acting on CB1Rs is able to enhance visual contrast sensitivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the URB597 behavioral experiments.

claim: The finding that drug-treated tadpoles exhibited superior detection of mesopic, but not photopic, visual stimuli strongly argues for a retinal site of action.
source: Although our observation of increased escape velocities suggests that the effects of WIN 55,212-2 were not limited to the retina, the finding that drug-treated tadpoles exhibited superior detection of mesopic, but not photopic, visual stimuli, strongly argues for a retinal site of action.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects under photopic vs mesopic conditions.

claim: The enhanced excitability of RGCs by CB1R activation likely contributes to the improvement in the visual detection of dim objects.
source: It is therefore highly likely that the enhanced excitability of RGCs by CB1R activation which we first report here, also contributes to this remarkable improvement in the visual detection of dim objects.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: Activation of CB1Rs on RGCs reduces [Cl−]i through the AMPK-dependent inhibition of NKCC1.
source: We found that activation of CB1Rs on RGCs reduces [Cl−]i, through the AMPK-dependent inhibition of NKCC1.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding supported by multiple experiments.

claim: Reduction in [Cl−]i results in the hyperpolarization of the RGC resting membrane potential by enhancing the driving force for Cl− currents through GlyRs.
source: This results in the hyperpolarization of the RGC resting membrane potential by enhancing the driving force for Cl− currents through GlyRs, and acutely enhances the intrinsic excitability of the RGCs, most likely through the resultant de-inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding supported by multiple experiments.

claim: The enhancement in RGC intrinsic excitability leads to the recruitment of additional, initially subthreshold RGC responses by target neurons in the optic tectum.
source: This enhancement in RGC intrinsic excitability leads to the recruitment of additional, initially subthreshold RGC responses by target neurons in the optic tectum, which in turn may contribute to improved visual contrast sensitivity.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding supported by multiple experiments.

claim: CB1Rs constitute one of the most highly expressed G-protein-coupled receptors in the central nervous system.
source: CB1Rs constitute one of the most highly expressed G-protein-coupled receptors in the central nervous system (Herkenham et al., 1990), where they generally have been reported to act to reduce neurotransmitter release by attenuating voltage-dependent Ca2+ or K+ conductances in presynaptic terminals (Chevaleyre et al., 2006; Kano et al., 2009; Piomelli, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CB1Rs generally act to reduce neurotransmitter release by attenuating voltage-dependent Ca2+ or K+ conductances in presynaptic terminals.
source: CB1Rs constitute one of the most highly expressed G-protein-coupled receptors in the central nervous system (Herkenham et al., 1990), where they generally have been reported to act to reduce neurotransmitter release by attenuating voltage-dependent Ca2+ or K+ conductances in presynaptic terminals (Chevaleyre et al., 2006; Kano et al., 2009; Piomelli, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CB1R-mediated hyperpolarization has been proposed to reduce intrinsic excitability in cerebellar and cortical interneurons by positive modulation of a K+ conductance.
source: CB1R-mediated hyperpolarization has also been proposed to reduce intrinsic excitability in cerebellar and cortical interneurons by positive modulation of a K+ conductance (Bacci et al., 2004; Kreitzer et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: This work presents a novel mechanism for interaction between glycinergic inhibition and the eCB system involving the regulation of Cl− homeostasis to enhance intrinsic neuronal excitability.
source: Our work presents a novel mechanism for interaction between glycinergic inhibition and the eCB system involving the regulation of Cl− homeostasis, to enhance intrinsic neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the novelty of the findings.

claim: In neurons, Cl− levels are primarily controlled by the interplay of the inward NKCC1 and outward KCC2 cation-Cl− co-transporters, which are modulated by phosphorylation.
source: In neurons, Cl− levels are primarily controlled by the interplay of the inward NKCC1 and outward KCC2 cation-Cl− co-transporters, which are modulated by phosphorylation (Darman et al., 2001; de Los Heros et al., 2006; Delpire and Austin, 2010; Garzón-Muvdi et al., 2007; Rinehart et al., 2009; Song et al., 2002; Wenz et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activation of human NKCC1 requires phosphorylation at T217 by SPAK family members downstream of WNK1.
source: Activation of human NKCC1 requires phosphorylation at T217 by SPAK family members downstream of WNK1 (Darman et al., 2001; Vitari et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: AMPK activation can result in the inhibition of human NKCC1 through phosphorylation at S77, as well as suppression of T217 phosphorylation by SPAK.
source: It had previously been reported that AMPK activation can result in the inhibition of human NKCC1 through phosphorylation at S77, as well as suppression of T217 phosphorylation by SPAK (Fraser et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Tonic glycinergic inhibition has been well studied in the spinal cord and hippocampus.
source: Although tonic glycinergic inhibition has been well studied in the spinal cord and hippocampus (Xu and Gong, 2010), our study is one of the first to suggest a role for tonic inhibition by strychnine-sensitive GlyRs in the retina.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: This study is one of the first to suggest a role for tonic inhibition by strychnine-sensitive GlyRs in the retina.
source: Although tonic glycinergic inhibition has been well studied in the spinal cord and hippocampus (Xu and Gong, 2010), our study is one of the first to suggest a role for tonic inhibition by strychnine-sensitive GlyRs in the retina.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: GlyRs have been reported to be directly positively modulated by cannabinoids.
source: Additionally, GlyRs have been reported to be directly positively modulated by cannabinoids (Lozovaya et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Suppression of HVA Ca2+ currents has been reported in dissociated rat RGCs.
source: Cannabinoid regulation of RGC-firing properties is not entirely unprecedented. Suppression of HVA Ca2+ currents has been reported in dissociated rat RGCs (Lalonde et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: RGCs express both the synthetic (NAPE-PLD) and degradative (FAAH) enzymes for AEA.
source: Interestingly, RGCs are known to express both the synthetic (NAPE-PLD) and degradative (FAAH) enzymes for AEA (Maione et al., 2009; Yazulla et al., 1999), suggesting they also may be a source of eCBs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The CB1R-dependent reduction in synaptic drive from bipolar and amacrine interneurons can be induced by direct RGC membrane depolarization.
source: In support of this idea, the CB1R-dependent reduction in synaptic drive from bipolar and amacrine interneurons can be induced by direct RGC membrane depolarization (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: AEA release acts in an auto- or paracrine manner to enhance RGC excitability.
source: Based on our present data, we propose that AEA release additionally acts in an auto- or paracrine manner to enhance RGC excitability.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Opposing actions on bipolar cell terminals and RGCs may serve to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of visual responses.
source: Opposing actions on bipolar cell terminals and RGCs may serve a useful role to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of visual responses by maintaining a vigorous retinal output while attenuating excessive synaptic noise from the outer retina (Grimes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed functional interpretation supported by citation.

claim: CB1R activation dramatically improved behavioral responses to dark moving cues near absolute threshold for visual detection.
source: This may explain our finding that CB1R activation dramatically improved behavioral responses to dark moving cues near absolute threshold for visual detection.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data.

claim: The mechanism described is reminiscent of the 'Westheimer effect' where detection sensitivity for a small test flash at the center of a background disk improves as the background disk increases in size.
source: Finally, our work describes a mechanism of sensitization to spatial subfield stimulation when a conditioning stimulus is presented in the periphery. This is reminiscent of the so-called 'Westheimer effect' where detection sensitivity for a small test flash at the center of a background disk improves as the background disk increases in size, an effect shown in humans (Westheimer, 1965) and lower vertebrates (Burkhardt, 1974).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Recent research has revealed that sensitization to temporal contrast changes can last for seconds in individual regions of the RGC surround field and may mediate a predictive function.
source: However, important limitations to this model exist (Essock et al., 1985; Sinai et al., 1999) and recent research has revealed that sensitization to temporal contrast changes can last for seconds in individual regions of the RGC surround field and may therefore mediate a predictive function (Kastner and Baccus, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The CB1R-dependent sensitization of mesopic RGC responses can persist for minutes but appears to require prolonged stimulation in the periphery to produce the eCBs that induce it.
source: The CB1R-dependent sensitization of mesopic RGC responses that we report here can persist for minutes, but appears to require prolonged stimulation in the periphery to produce the eCBs that induce it.
evidence: This is supported by the conditioning stimulation experiments.

claim: This mechanism may be beneficial as a means of optimizing RGC signal-to-noise ratios during the initial period of dark adaptation before photoreceptors obtain maximum sensitivity.
source: This mechanism may be beneficial as a means of optimizing RGC signal-to-noise ratios during the initial period of dark adaptation before photoreceptors obtain maximum sensitivity.
evidence: This is a proposed functional interpretation of the findings.

claim: The CB1R-dependent mechanism for low luminance sensitization described in the developing amphibian retina will require additional investigation to determine whether it also occurs in the mammalian eye.
source: The CB1R-dependent mechanism for low luminance sensitization that we describe here in the developing amphibian retina will require additional investigation to determine whether it also occurs in the mammalian eye, although the psychophysical evidence is encouraging (Russo et al., 2004; West, 1991).
evidence: This acknowledges the need for future studies and cites supporting psychophysical evidence.
